sunsetPlanner.title: Sunset & blue hour
sunsetPlanner.note: Arrive about 60 minutes before sunset. Roughly 30 minutes after sunset the bridge and riverside glow — prime time for photos. The blue hour (about 20–30 min after sunset) frames sky and steel together, most photogenic.
sunsetPlanner.seaGlare: Lighting tip: the bridge is most photogenic in the soft light just before and after sunset; midday is harsh and busy.
sunsetPlanner.tideTip: Crowd tip: early morning and the hour before sunset are calmest; midday is hottest and busiest.

trainCrossings.title: Watching a train cross the bridge
trainCrossings.description: A train crossing the bridge is the highlight of a visit. Services run several times a day in each direction and cross slowly, so you have time to see the whole structure flex. The times below are a planning guide only — confirm them locally before you build a day around them.
trainCrossings.warning: Important: trains are frequently delayed, so treat these times as a rough guide. Be behind the refuge points at least 20 minutes ahead, never stand on the rails for a photo, and check the current timetable locally. The schedule is subject to change.

etiquetteSafety.title: Etiquette & safety tips
etiquetteSafety.subtitle: A few small rules so visitors and the memory of the place are both respected.

rules.title: Remember its meaning
rules.text: Tens of thousands died building the railway. Many visitors keep a quiet, reflective tone, and the memorial markers here are graves or commemorative sites — never move or lean on them.

rules.title: Ask before posing
rules.text: Photos are welcome, but avoid careless or jokey poses on a site of remembrance. Drones need permission.

rules.title: Mind the walkway, never stand on the tracks
rules.text: Keep bags in front in crowds, stay clear of the rails, and step behind the refuge platforms when a train approaches — trains cross without warning and cannot stop quickly. Keep children within arm's reach at all times.

rules.title: Take everything back out
rules.text: The bridge and riverbanks have limited waste collection. Carry out bottles, wrappers and food scraps — plastic in the river is the most visible damage visitors cause.

rules.title: Do not feed the animals
rules.text: Macaques, monitor lizards and river birds quickly become dependent on handouts, and fed animals can turn aggressive. Watch from a distance and never feed by hand.

rules.title: Respect local places of worship
rules.text: Nearby temples and shrines are working religious sites. Cover shoulders and knees, remove shoes where indicated, and ask before photographing people at prayer.

rules.title: Support locally, and fairly
rules.text: Riverside vendors, family-run shops and small museums are part of the community: agree prices, tip modestly if you are happy, and do not buy objects presented as wartime relics.

intro.title: About River Kwai Bridge (Kanchanaburi)
intro.equalStatement: Welcome to River Kwai Bridge (สะพานข้ามแม่น้ำแคว), widely recognized as the central Kwai Bridge. Located in the heart of Kanchanaburi, Kanchanaburi Province, Thailand, this destination serves as a primary hub for travellers visiting the region.
intro.nearbyStatement: When visiting River Kwai Bridge, visitors can easily explore surrounding historical landmarks and points of interest, including Kanchanaburi War Cemetery (Don Rak) and Hellfire Pass Memorial.
intro.description: The River Kwai Bridge is part of the Burma–Thailand (Death) Railway, built by Imperial Japan between 1942 and 1943 to link Thailand with Burma. Constructed under brutal conditions by Allied prisoners of war and tens of thousands of Asian forced labourers, the line became known for the enormous human cost of its construction. The bridge you see today is a reconstruction: parts were destroyed in Allied bombing and rebuilt after the war. Trains still run across it, and the riverbanks have become a place where history, daily life, and remembrance meet.

bestTime.text: Cool season (Nov–Feb) is most pleasant for walking the bridge. Hot season (Mar–May) is very warm — go after 16:00. Rainy season (Jun–Oct) brings showers; the river is fullest and the hills greenest.

siteNotes.title: Management & public order
siteNotes.text: The bridge sits at the meeting point of railway, tourism, and local community. The State Railway of Thailand operates the active line, the Tourism Authority of Thailand promotes the site, and Kanchanaburi Province manages local infrastructure and the annual River Kwai Bridge Week. Riverside vendors and museums keep the area welcoming. Please follow on-site guidance and visit respectfully.

historyIntro.title: History & Significance of River Kwai Bridge
historyIntro.subtitle: The bridge: then and now — from a wartime strategic line to a symbol remembered around the world.

historyStory.intro: The bridge is one link in a 415-kilometre railway built between Thailand and Burma under Japanese occupation. Why it was built, how fast it went up, and what it cost are the keys to reading everything you see here.

sections.title: Why a railway through the jungle
sections.content: Japan needed a secure land route to supply its forces in Burma once the sea lanes became dangerous. In June 1942 work began on a line linking Nong Pla Duk, in Ban Pong district, with Thanbyuzayat in Burma — a route earlier surveyors had judged impractical.

sections.title: Forced labour at impossible speed
sections.content: Around 60,000 Allied prisoners of war — British, Dutch, Australian and American — and some 200,000 Asian labourers, most of them Burmese, Malayan, Tamil and Javanese men recruited or conscripted by the Japanese, were moved onto the line. The original estimate was five years; the railway was finished in roughly sixteen months, driven by pressure rather than machinery. About 12,000 Allied prisoners and an estimated 90,000 Asian labourers died.

sections.title: Two bridges in one place
sections.content: A temporary wooden trestle bridge opened in February 1943, with a steel bridge alongside it in April 1943, carrying the railway across the Khwae Yai towards the Three Pagodas Pass. The two stood side by side, the wooden one taking the first trains while the steel one carried the heavy loads. The steel spans were not designed for this site: they were dismantled from bridges in Java and shipped to Thailand, then reassembled by hand.

sections.title: Bombed, repaired, bombed again
sections.content: The bridge was a bottleneck for the whole line, so Allied aircraft attacked it repeatedly, and two spans of the steel bridge were dropped into the river. After the war it was repaired and put back into service. What you walk across today is a mix of original wartime steel and post-war replacement spans — still carrying scheduled trains.

sections.title: A film that rewrote the story
sections.content: Pierre Boulle's novel became David Lean's Oscar-winning film, shot largely in Sri Lanka rather than Thailand. Its fictional bridge, its fictional colonel and its heroic demolition never happened here. The film made the name world-famous and, unfairly, buried the real history of forced labour.

sections.title: How a river got renamed
sections.content: There was never a river called 'Kwai' at this crossing. The film's title was applied to a stretch of the Mae Klong, and in the 1960s that section was formally renamed Khwae Yai — the river effectively took its name from a film.

sections.title: Still a working railway, and a memorial
sections.content: Trains still cross the bridge as part of the Nam Tok line. When the war ended in 1945 most of the railway was abandoned and lifted, and only sections like this one survived. Around the bridge stand the Kanchanaburi War Cemetery, the Thailand–Burma Railway Centre and, deeper in the mountains, the Hellfire Pass Memorial — together the main places where the railway's dead are remembered and explained.

historyStory.legendsIntro: Much of what visitors 'know' about the bridge comes from a 1957 film. Here is what is documented, what is local story, and what is simply not true.

legends.title: Myth: the bridge was blown up by commandos
legends.text: There was no commando raid of that kind. The bridge was brought down by bombing from the air and was rebuilt afterwards — it still stands because it was repaired, not because it was never destroyed.

legends.title: Myth: the river is called the River Kwai
legends.text: The river crossing the bridge is the Khwae Yai, part of the Mae Klong system. The name 'River Kwai' spread from the film and was later adopted officially for this stretch — a rare case of fiction renaming geography.

legends.title: Myth: the film was shot here
legends.text: Almost none of it was. The bridge sequences were filmed at Kitulgala in Sri Lanka, with a full-size wooden bridge built for the purpose. Nothing on this river was used for the destruction sequence.

legends.title: Story: the steel came from Java
legends.text: The steel spans are widely reported to have come from a dismantled bridge in the Dutch East Indies and to have been shipped here in pieces. Whatever their exact origin, they were assembled by hand under wartime conditions — which is why the workmanship is visibly uneven.

legends.title: Story: the wooden bridge vanished
legends.text: Locals still point out where the temporary wooden bridge stood. It carried the first trains while the steel bridge was being finished, then was dismantled or lost to war damage — only its memory and the alignment remain.

legends.title: Local custom: quiet offerings at the trackside
legends.text: Railway workers and residents sometimes leave small offerings beside the line out of respect for those who died. If you see flowers, incense or small tokens, leave them undisturbed — they are memorials, not litter.

didYouKnow.title: Movie fiction vs. reality
didYouKnow.text: The 1957 Oscar-winning film made the bridge globally famous, but its story is fiction: the bridge sequences were shot in Sri Lanka, and no wartime destruction like the film's took place here. The real history of the Death Railway carries far more weight than the cinema version — which is why this page sets the record out in full.

deepGuide.title: The River Kwai Bridge in depth
deepGuide.subtitle: How to get here from Bangkok in detail, what else is worth your time nearby, and the practical details that make a visit easier.

sections.title: Bangkok to the bridge, in detail
sections.lead: There is a railway halt at the bridge itself, so on the train you can step off within a few minutes' walk of the span instead of going into Kanchanaburi town and doubling back.

blocks.text: The train is the arrival most visitors remember, because the final stretch follows the old Death Railway alignment. Departures are from Thonburi station, also called Bangkok Noi, on the Nam Tok line — note that this is a different station from Wongwian Yai, which serves the Mahachai line south to Samut Sakhon and does not go to Kanchanaburi. Allow roughly 2.5 to 3 hours. Beyond Kanchanaburi station the line crosses the river at its own halt, สะพานแม่น้ำแคว (River Kwai Bridge), on the way toward Nam Tok.

Third-class carriages are cheap and open-windowed, and some services carry air-conditioned tourist carriages at a higher fare. Trains are few — only a small number each way per day, and the last return toward Bangkok leaves in the afternoon — so check the current timetable with the State Railway of Thailand before committing, and consider staying a night in Kanchanaburi rather than day-tripping.

Buses and minivans from Bangkok's Southern Bus Terminal (Sai Tai Mai) are more frequent and less likely to sell out, running through the day, and take 2–3 hours depending on traffic leaving the city. Minivans are faster but more cramped. Either way you arrive at Kanchanaburi's bus station and take a songthaew, taxi or ride-hailing car the last few kilometres to the bridge.

By car, the usual route is Route 4 (Phet Kasem) west and then Route 323 into Kanchanaburi, around 130 km and 2–3 hours. Parking sits along the road and at riverside restaurants close to the bridge. Guided day tours from Bangkok are the least flexible option but remove all logistics if you have only one day; most combine the bridge with the war cemetery and a museum.

sections.title: What else is worth your time nearby
sections.lead: The bridge is one stop on a railway and one point on a river. Almost everything that gives it meaning lies within an hour or two.

items.name: Kanchanaburi War Cemetery (Don Rak)
items.text: The main Commonwealth cemetery for the railway, holding nearly 7,000 graves and maintained by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission. Flat, quiet and free to enter.
items.tip: Go in the cooler part of the day; there is little shade.

items.name: Thailand–Burma Railway Centre
items.text: A modern, carefully curated museum covering the railway's construction and the people who built it. The clearest single explanation of what happened here.
items.tip: Visit this before the bridge if you want the site to make sense.

items.name: JEATH War Museum
items.text: The older, rougher museum next to the bridge, housed in a reconstruction of a prisoner-of-war hut. Less polished than the Railway Centre, more atmospheric.
items.tip: Cheap, close, and easy to add to a bridge visit.

items.name: Wampo Viaduct (Tham Krasae)
items.text: A wooden trestle hugging the cliff above the river: the most dramatic surviving stretch of the railway, and the section most visitors photograph without knowing its name.
items.tip: Reachable by train; walking the trestle is the highlight.

items.name: Hellfire Pass Memorial Museum
items.text: The cutting that prisoners excavated by hand, now an Australian-funded memorial with a walking trail down through the pass. The most affecting site on the whole line.
items.tip: Needs the better part of a day; start early and carry water.

items.name: Erawan National Park
items.text: A seven-tier limestone waterfall with turquoise pools, set in forest northwest of Kanchanaburi. A natural counterweight to the history.
items.tip: Swimming is allowed in the lower tiers; the upper ones are a steep climb.

sections.title: Practical facts before you go
sections.lead: The bridge is open, free and unstaffed — which is exactly why a little preparation changes the visit.

items.label: Entry
items.note: No ticket and no gate. Nearby museums charge separately.

items.label: Hours
items.note: The bridge is part of a working railway, not a ticketed attraction.

items.label: Time needed
items.note: For the bridge and riverside alone; half a day with a museum and the cemetery.

items.label: Best light
items.note: Golden hour on the steel, once the heat has broken.

items.label: Busiest
items.note: Coach groups cluster around midday, especially in the cool season.

items.label: Access
items.note: The riverside is easy; the bridge walkway is uneven in places.

blocks.text: Walk the bridge rather than only photographing it from the bank. There is a wooden walkway beside the rails with refuge bays where you can stand aside as a train passes. Stay inside the bays while a train is moving, hold children's hands, and watch your footing on the sleepers and the gaps between them.

Late November to early December brings River Kwai Bridge Week, when the province stages a sound-and-light event recalling the bridge's wartime history. It is the liveliest the site ever gets, and the most crowded. Outside that period, early morning and the two hours before sunset are the calmest times to be there.

Bring cash: the small museums, riverside vendors and songthaews generally do not take cards. Sun protection matters more than it looks, because the bridge is fully exposed and the reflected heat off the steel and water is considerable in the middle of the day.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.subtitle: The most-asked things about the River Kwai Bridge.

items.q: Where is River Kwai Bridge located?
items.a: River Kwai Bridge is located in Tha Ma Kham, Mueang Kanchanaburi District, Kanchanaburi 71000, Thailand — on the south bank of the Khwae Yai, about 3 km from central Kanchanaburi.

items.q: Is it River Kwai Bridge or River Khwae Bridge?
items.a: Both names mean the same bridge. “Khwae” (แคว) is the correct Thai romanisation, so River Khwae Bridge is the more accurate spelling and the form used by the State Railway of Thailand and heritage bodies. “River Kwai” spread worldwide through the 1957 film and remains the most common search term, so you will see both on signs and maps. The river it crosses is the Khwae Yai, and the Thai name of the bridge is สะพานข้ามแม่น้ำแคว.

items.q: How do I get to River Kwai Bridge from Bangkok?
items.a: Three practical options. By train: from Thonburi station (Bangkok Noi) on the Nam Tok line, roughly 2.5–3 hours to Kanchanaburi and unaffected by road traffic — the bridge has its own halt on the Nam Tok side of Kanchanaburi station, so you can step off within a few minutes' walk of the span. By minivan or bus: from Mo Chit, Sai Tai Mai or the Kanchanaburi-bound vans, about 2–3 hours. By car or taxi: around 130 km via Route 4 (Phet Kasem) then Route 323, roughly 2–3 hours depending on Bangkok traffic.

items.q: Is River Kwai Bridge free to visit?
items.a: Yes — River Kwai Bridge is a public space and is free to visit year-round. Only the nearby museums may charge a small entry fee.

items.q: What is the exact address and postal code?
items.a: River Kwai Rd, Tha Ma Kham, Mueang Kanchanaburi District, Kanchanaburi 71000, Thailand. Google Maps Plus Code: 2GR3+QM Ban Tai, Mueang Kanchanaburi District.

items.q: What is the Google Maps rating of River Kwai Bridge?
items.a: River Kwai Bridge holds a 4.6 / 5 rating on Google Maps, based on 14,890 user reviews (latest). Ratings and reviews are sourced from Google Maps users.
The bridge and riverside are accessible around the clock; trains run on a daytime schedule, so plan around them.
No — walking across the bridge is free. Nearby museums may charge a small fee.
Mornings and the hour before sunset are coolest and best lit; midday is hot and busy.
It is part of the WWII Death Railway, built by POWs and forced labourers; the 1957 film fixed its name in global memory.

items.q: Can you still ride a train across?
items.a: Yes — the State Railway of Thailand runs passenger services on the line.

items.q: What happened to the original bridge?
items.a: Parts were destroyed in wartime bombing and rebuilt after the war; it still carries trains.
Train or bus to Kanchanaburi (2–3 hrs), then a short taxi or songthaew to the bridge.

items.q: Hard to get a ride back?
items.a: Pre-book Grab/Bolt, or walk to the main road for a songthaew; off-peak is easier.
About 3 km from central Kanchanaburi; a few minutes by songthaew.

items.q: Is the bridge walkway wheelchair / stroller friendly?
items.a: Partly. The walkway runs on open sleepers with gaps between them and no side barriers, so wheelchairs and strollers need care; the north-bank riverside promenade is level and easier for those who need it.
Yes, with supervision — keep children close, mind the gaps between sleepers and the open sides, and step aside well before a train passes.

items.q: Any walking cautions on the bridge?
items.a: Wear closed shoes; heels can catch in the sleeper gaps, and the sides are open with no rail — don't lean or climb over. Step aside for trains.

alerts.thunder: Thunderstorms are forecast. Keep off the open bridge spans and away from the riverbank while they pass — do not shelter under trees or stand on high ground.
alerts.heavyRain: Heavy rain is on the way, around {rain} mm over the next 12 hours. Avoid the river channel, low ground and the valleys, and watch for flash flooding.
alerts.wind: Strong wind, force {level}, with gusts near {gust} km/h. Hold the handrail on the bridge and stay clear of loose signage and the rocky riverbank.
alerts.heat: Serious heat, up to {max}°C. Move the heavy walking to early morning, stay in shade at midday and carry more water than you think you need.
alerts.fog: Fog with visibility around {visibility} km. River crossings and road journeys can be delayed, and the long views will be lost — not the day for the postcard shot.
alerts.riverRise: Heavy rain upstream, around {rain} mm. River levels can rise and turn muddy at short notice — stay off the sandbars and do not swim.
alerts.fireRisk: High fire risk: humidity near {humidity}%, no rain on the way and hot, breezy air. No fires, no smoking and no naked flames in the wooded areas.
alerts.tempSwing: A swing of about {drop}°C between day and night. Carry a light layer you can add or remove.

weather.adviceTitle: What this means for your visit

outfit.hot: Around {max}°C and climbing — light, breathable clothing, and keep the long walks for first thing in the morning or after 16:00.
outfit.humid: Humid with it, near {humidity}% — quick-drying fabrics will be far more comfortable.
outfit.cold: Cool for this region at about {max}°C — bring a proper jacket, especially for the early start and the river at dusk.
outfit.cool: Mild at around {max}°C — long sleeves and a light outer layer are comfortable all day.
outfit.mild: Pleasant, roughly {min}–{max}°C — ordinary light clothing, with a thin layer for the evening.
outfit.tempDrop: Day and night differ by about {drop}°C — a light jacket you can put on or take off is the practical choice.
outfit.uv: UV index around {uv} — cover up, use sunscreen and keep to shade between 11:00 and 15:00.
outfit.rain: Rain is in the picture — water-resistant or quick-drying clothes work better than an umbrella on an open bridge.
outfit.windy: Breezy at force {level} — skip wide skirts and loose scarves, and secure anything light.

plan.thunder: Thunderstorms during the day — skip the open walkways and the river, and move to the museums and the railway centre instead.
plan.heavyRain: Not a day for outdoor sightseeing — river boats and outdoor attractions may close, so build the day around indoor stops.
plan.rainLikely: A good chance of rain at about {chance}% — keep the plan flexible and have an indoor fallback ready.
plan.lightRain: Showers look possible rather than constant — outdoor time is fine, just shorten the exposed stretches and shelter when it builds.
plan.heat: Very hot at around {max}°C — walk the bridge at first light or after 16:00 and treat midday as indoor time.
plan.clear: Clear skies — excellent for outdoor sightseeing, and the best conditions for sunrise and sunset views.
plan.overcast: Soft, even light with no glare — genuinely good for photography and for long, unhurried exploring.
plan.fog: Poor visibility, around {visibility} km — the long views over the river and hills will be gone, so plan a shorter, closer visit.
plan.wind: Wind at force {level} — river boats and open-air activities may be suspended, and the exposed bridge spans feel rougher.
plan.uvStrong: Strong UV at index {uv} — shorten the midday outdoor stretch and stick to the shaded riverside.
plan.riverCalm: The river is calm and low with little wind — the best conditions of the week for riverside photography and reflections.
plan.pleasant: Reasonably settled — an easy day for the bridge, the banks and the war cemetery.

gear.raincoat: Light rain jacket — better than a long umbrella in wind
gear.outerwear: A light layer for the evening
gear.shoes: Shoes with grip — the sleepers and riverbank turn slippery
gear.mask: A mask if you are sensitive to poor air
gear.repellent: Insect repellent for the riverside at dusk

weather.envNote: Indicative readings worked out from the forecast, not measurements taken on site — use them to decide how hard to push the day.

riverRise.name: River rise risk
riverRise.low: No rain of note upstream — the river is steady and clear.
riverRise.moderate: Some rain upstream — the water may rise and colour slightly. Keep an eye on the level.
riverRise.high: Heavy rain upstream — expect a fast, muddy rise. Stay off the sandbars and out of the water.

waterWind.name: Wind on the water
waterWind.low: The surface is calm — good for boats and for reflections.
waterWind.moderate: A working breeze — small boats will feel it and the surface will chop.
waterWind.high: Rough water — river trips may be suspended and small craft should stay in.

mosquito.name: Mosquito activity
mosquito.moderate: Noticeable near the water and at dusk — repellent is a good idea.
mosquito.high: Very active after the rain — cover up at dawn and dusk and use repellent.

fireRisk.name: Fire risk in the hills
fireRisk.low: Low risk — conditions are not favourable for fire.
fireRisk.moderate: Rising risk in the dry grass and woodland — no open flames.
fireRisk.high: High risk — no fires, no smoking and no burning off in the wooded areas.

heatStress.name: Heat stress
heatStress.low: Comfortable for walking and standing around.
heatStress.moderate: Noticeable heat — take regular breaks in shade and drink often.
heatStress.high: Serious heat load — limit outdoor time, rest often and watch for dizziness.

weather.fallbackTitle: Typical conditions for this time of year
weather.fallbackText: Live readings are refreshing. The bridge sits in a tropical savanna climate: warm to hot all year, wettest from June to October, a hot dry stretch from March to May, and the most comfortable weather from November to February.

seasonStrategy.title: Seasonal visit strategy
seasonStrategy.subtitle: Weather, river water and wildlife side by side, so you can choose when to come.
seasonStrategy.intro: Kanchanaburi has three recognisable seasons rather than four. The table below combines long-term monthly climate averages with the usual river and wildlife patterns recorded around the Khwae Yai — the practical way to decide what to pack and how hard to push each day.
seasonStrategy.note: Weather, water and wildlife are a combined reading of 30-year monthly climate normals (1991–2020) for the Kanchanaburi area, cross-checked against national meteorological and conservation records. River and wildlife notes describe typical seasonal behaviour, not measurements taken on any single day.

rows.name: Cool season
rows.weather: The most comfortable stretch: roughly 20–32 °C, low humidity, clear skies and almost no rain. Mornings and evenings can feel genuinely cool.
rows.water: The Khwae Yai runs low and clear, holding the deepest green water of the year — the best month for reflections and for seeing the pier structure.
rows.wildlife: Birds are most active along the river and in the hotel gardens, and the hills stay lush green well into December after the rains.
rows.crowds: The busiest of the three seasons, and the densest for festivals — come early in the morning if you want the walkway mostly to yourself.
rows.verdict: First-time visitors, photographers, walking the full bridge, combining with Erawan Falls or Hellfire Pass.

rows.name: Hot season
rows.weather: The hottest months: highs commonly 35–38 °C with strong midday sun and rising humidity. Occasional pre-monsoon storms arrive towards the end of the period.
rows.water: Water levels are at their lowest and the river turns shallow and slow; some waterfalls further upstream run dry.
rows.wildlife: Animals retreat into shade, so the best sightings are at dawn and dusk rather than midday. Dust and dry grass dominate the hills.
rows.crowds: Quieter than the cool season; the bridge is both coolest and least busy before 10:00 and after 16:00.
rows.verdict: Early-morning visits, the war cemetery and indoor museums, hot springs or riverside hotel time.

rows.name: Rainy season
rows.weather: Warm and humid with frequent heavy showers, usually arriving as intense afternoon bursts rather than all-day drizzle. September and October are the wettest.
rows.water: The river swells, runs fast and turns turbid brown — dramatic to photograph, but not safe to swim in.
rows.wildlife: Peak greenery, loudest birdsong and the most visible insects and lizards. Waterfalls and reservoirs are at their fullest.
rows.crowds: The quietest of the three — you will often share the walkway with only a handful of people, and riverside rooms are at their cheapest.
rows.verdict: Green landscapes, dramatic river photography, low-season prices and thinner crowds.

visitRoutes.title: Recommended routes: half day or full day
visitRoutes.subtitle: Two ready-to-follow itineraries — one for a quick stop, one that covers the story properly.
visitRoutes.disclaimer: Routes are experience-based outlines. Actual train times, museum hours and transport depend on conditions on the day.

half.name: Half day at the bridge
half.goodFor: Travellers passing through, families, first-time visitors
half.summary: Enough time to walk the bridge, see it from both banks and understand the story without rushing — or fighting the heat.

steps.title: Arrive early and walk the span
steps.text: Cool air, soft light and few people. Walk from the eastern end towards the western bank, pausing at the refuge points and reading the plaques as you go.

steps.title: Both banks, two vantage points
steps.text: Cross to the far bank for the classic full-curve view, then come back down to river level for the low angle under the spans.

steps.title: Watch a train cross
steps.text: Stand well clear of the track. Trains move slowly across the bridge, which gives you time to see the whole structure flex as they pass.

steps.title: Museum and war cemetery
steps.text: A short look at the bridge-side museum or the Thailand–Burma Railway Centre, then a quiet 30 minutes at the Kanchanaburi War Cemetery.

steps.title: Riverside lunch
steps.text: Eat by the water, then head on — you have covered the essentials before the heat of the day.

steps.title: Optional: return for golden hour
steps.text: If you are staying nearby, come back before sunset for the best light and the calmest atmosphere on the water.

full.name: Full day: the bridge and the railway
full.goodFor: History-minded travellers, photographers, anyone with their own transport or a hired driver
full.summary: Pairs the bridge with the two places that explain it: the war cemetery in town and the Hellfire Pass cutting in the mountains.

steps.title: Sunrise at the bridge
steps.text: The quietest and coolest hour, with mist on the water in the cool season. Photograph before the crowds arrive.

steps.title: Breakfast and the riverside
steps.text: Refuel locally, then walk the full length of the bridge and both approaches at an easy pace.

steps.title: Kanchanaburi War Cemetery
steps.text: Close to 7,000 Commonwealth and Dutch graves, laid out with deliberate symmetry. Allow 30–45 minutes.

steps.title: Ride the Death Railway
steps.text: Take the train towards Nam Tok for the river viaduct section — the most scenic stretch of the line.

steps.title: Lunch near the line
steps.text: Eat where the train stops, then continue by road towards the mountains.

steps.title: Hellfire Pass Memorial
steps.text: Walk down into the cutting that was carved by hand, and visit the museum at the top. Allow 1.5–2 hours.

steps.title: Return for golden hour
steps.text: Back at the bridge for the late light, then dinner by the river.

audiencePlans.title: Plans tailored to who you're travelling with
audiencePlans.subtitle: Four quick profiles, then three ready-made plans — pick the one that matches your group and the pace you want.

groups.tip: Tripod just before sunset; bank and bridge both shoot well.
Pair the bridge with the museums and cemetery.
Riverside cafés near the bridge serve with a view.
Avoid peaks, take breaks, watch the little ones.

items.name: Families with children
items.tagline: Short, safe and full of small discoveries
includes: Walk the main span and stop at the riverside viewing terraces
Watch a train cross — the moment children remember most
A short stroll to the riverside cafés and stalls
Optional: the small museum beside the bridge for a 20-minute look
tips: Hold hands on the walkway — the gaps between the sleepers open straight down to the river
Come before 10:00 or after 16:00 to avoid the hottest hours
Bring water, hats and a spare set of clothes in the rainy season
items.watchOut: There is no barrier along the walkway edge and the surface is uneven steel and timber sleepers, so scooters, wheeled toys and open sandals are best left behind.

items.name: Photographers & nature lovers
includes: Blue hour and sunrise from the western bank
Framing the bridge through the sleepers and along the river bends
Midday: the war cemetery and riverside markets for context shots
Golden hour from the opposite bank, then dusk with the bridge lights
tips: A wide lens covers the full curve; a short telephoto catches trains, rivets and people on the span
The best reflections need low water and no wind — cool-season mornings
Bring a cloth: river spray and dust settle on the glass surprisingly fast
items.watchOut: Never photograph from the tracks themselves — trains cross without warning. Stay on the pedestrian side, behind the refuge points.

items.name: Low mobility & step-free visits
items.tagline: See the bridge properly without climbing
includes: The level riverside promenade and viewing areas at the bridge approach
Ground-level viewpoints on both banks for the classic photograph
Seating and shade within a short, even distance
Optional: a slow drive along the river road for changing angles
tips: Vehicle drop-off is possible close to the bridge entrance — ask the driver to stop there rather than at the car park
Mornings are cooler and much quieter, with more room to move
A companion is recommended if you plan to go onto the bridge itself
items.watchOut: The bridge deck is historic steel with open gaps between the sleepers and no handrail at the walkway edge. Many visitors take in the whole structure from the banks instead, which is just as rewarding.

facilities.title: Visitor services & nearby amenities
facilities.subtitle: What's available around the bridge, described by category rather than by business.
facilities.neutralNote: This is an independent, non-commercial guide. We describe the kinds of services you will find nearby and we do not recommend, rank or link to individual businesses.

items.name: Public toilets
items.note: Basic facilities at the bridge approach and by the riverside food area. A small fee is normal, and paper often runs out — carry tissues.

items.name: Parking
items.note: Roadside spaces and small private car parks within a few minutes' walk. Weekends and holidays fill early; expect a modest fee for attended parking.

items.name: Food & drink
items.note: Riverside restaurants, noodle shops and street stalls, from a quick bowl to a full sit-down meal with a river view. Busiest after sunset.

items.name: Cafés
items.note: Several cafés with river terraces — useful for waiting out a shower or for late-afternoon shade.

items.name: Shops & convenience stores
items.note: Small groceries and convenience stores near the bridge for water, snacks and basics; larger supermarkets and a shopping centre in the town centre.

items.name: Accommodation
items.note: From riverside guesthouses and hostels to floating hotels and mid-range resorts, mostly within 10–20 minutes of the bridge. Book ahead in the cool season.

items.name: Pharmacy
items.note: Pharmacies cluster in the town centre. Bridge-side stalls sell drinks and snacks, not medicines, so stock up before you go.

items.name: Medical help
items.note: A provincial hospital and several clinics sit in Kanchanaburi town, roughly 10–15 minutes away. For an emergency in Thailand dial 1669.

items.name: ATMs & cash
items.note: ATMs are available near the bridge and in town. Many small stalls and some transport still prefer cash, so keep some baht on you.

items.name: Fuel & EV charging
items.note: Fuel stations line the main roads into town, and some larger stations and hotels have electric-vehicle charging points. There are none on the bridge approach itself, so plan ahead.

items.name: Baby care
items.note: No dedicated nursing room at the bridge. Riverside restaurants and the town-centre shopping centre are the practical places to feed and change a baby.

items.name: Mobile signal & Wi-Fi
items.note: Mobile data coverage is generally good around the bridge. Many cafés and hotels offer free Wi-Fi to customers.

items.name: Left luggage
items.note: No lockers at the bridge. Hotels and guesthouses will usually hold bags for guests, and some town-centre shops offer paid storage.

items.name: Rain gear & essentials
items.note: Ponchos, hats, sunscreen and bottled water are sold by stalls near the entrance, especially through the rainy season.

bridgeInDetail.title: Reading the bridge
bridgeInDetail.subtitle: A short explainer for what you are actually looking at: the curve, the rivets, and the reasons behind both.
bridgeInDetail.explainTitle: How to read what you're looking at
bridgeInDetail.explainIntro: The bridge is a working piece of 1940s engineering, and its shape tells you what it had to do: carry heavy trains across a wide river, on a deadline that left no time to build a proper foundation first.

explainItems.title: A curved bridge, not a straight one
explainItems.text: The spans sit slightly off-axis so the track meets each bank at a gentler angle. Look along the walkway and you will see the curve — it is a response to the river bend, not a construction error.

explainItems.title: Riveted steel plate girders
explainItems.text: The main spans are riveted steel, joined plate by plate. Riveting was the standard way to hold steel together before on-site welding became reliable, and it is still visible as rows of small domes along every beam.

explainItems.title: There used to be two bridges
explainItems.text: A temporary wooden trestle bridge and a steel bridge stood side by side. The wooden structure carried the first trains while the steel one took the heavy loads. Only the steel bridge survives today.

explainItems.title: Why the water looks different every season
explainItems.text: In the cool season the Khwae Yai runs low and clear, so the pier bases and the riverbed structure become visible. In the rainy season it carries sediment and rises fast — which is why the piers are set so deep and so wide.

explainItems.title: It is still a live railway
explainItems.text: This is not a museum piece: passenger trains still cross on a regular daytime schedule. That is why the walkway has refuge platforms — they exist so you have somewhere safe to stand when a train arrives.

explainItems.title: Why trains crawl through here
explainItems.text: The alignment through the mountains is tight and steep, so trains slow to walking pace across the bridge and through the cuttings. That slowness is a direct result of how quickly the line was built.
